meta.title: Quantization, Distillation, and Inference Optimization
meta.thesis: Quantization, distillation, and inference optimization reduce cost or latency in different ways, so the right choice depends on whether the bottleneck is memory, model size, serving throughput, or quality retention.

mentalMap.title: Inference optimization — memory, model, and serving levers
mentalMap.caption: The map compares quantization, distillation, and runtime tactics by what bottleneck they solve.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Optimize only after quality works: quantization reduces representation cost, distillation changes the model, and serving tactics improve throughput.

nodes.sub: Build the simplest useful picture of Quantization, Distillation, and Inference Optimization.
nodes.what: Measurement identifies whether memory, compute, or routing is the problem.
nodes.relevance: It prevents making a cheaper system that silently gets worse.

nodes.label: Quantization
nodes.sub: See the moving parts and how they interact.
nodes.what: Quantization stores model values with fewer bits.
nodes.relevance: It is the first lever when the same model fits poorly or costs too much.
nodes.orient: How lower-bit weights reduce memory while risking task quality.

nodes.label: Distillation
nodes.sub: Make the choices that change quality, cost, or risk.
nodes.what: Distillation transfers behavior into a different model.
nodes.relevance: It is useful when repeated internal tasks do not need the largest model.
nodes.orient: How a smaller student learns a teacher’s behavior on known workloads.

nodes.sub: Connect the concept to a small practical artifact.
nodes.what: Serving optimization changes how requests flow through the system.
nodes.relevance: It can reduce latency without altering model weights.
nodes.orient: How batching, cache, routing, and token limits change runtime behavior.

nodes.label: Quality per dollar
nodes.sub: Use active recall and a decision checklist to make it stick.
nodes.what: The final metric combines quality, latency, and cost.

modules.title: Start with the bottleneck, not the trick
modules.sub: Before optimizing, establish quality and runtime baselines.
modules.summary: Optimization is only useful if you know what you are optimizing and what quality must be preserved.
objectives: Name baseline metrics for inference optimization.
Separate memory, latency, throughput, and quality issues.

blocks.title: Optimization without evals is guesswork

spans.text: The first step is a baseline: task quality, p50/p95 latency, tokens per second, memory use, cost per request, and failure slices. Without that, a cheaper model can quietly damage the product.
Problem anchor: a support summarizer is accurate with a 13B model but too slow for live chat. The team must reduce latency without losing escalation details.

blocks.analogy: Optimization is like tightening bolts on a machine; first find which part is actually rattling.

blocks.title: Baseline card for the support summarizer

items.text: Quality: 91% rubric pass on held-out chats.
Latency: p95 is 5.8 seconds; target is 2.5 seconds.
Memory: full-precision model consumes too much VRAM for desired batch size.
Risk: summaries must preserve refund amounts and escalation reason.

blocks.title: Check baseline

options.text: A quality and runtime baseline on realistic examples.
A promise that smaller is always faster.

blocks.explanation: Optimization decisions need measured bottlenecks and quality tolerance.

modules.title: Quantization: fewer bits for the same model
modules.sub: If memory or bandwidth is the bottleneck, reduce representation size.
modules.summary: Quantization can lower VRAM and bandwidth by representing weights or activations with fewer bits, but quality and speed depend on method and hardware.
objectives: Evaluate quantized quality against full precision.

blocks.title: Quantization compresses numeric representation

spans.text: Quantization maps high-precision values into lower-bit formats such as 8-bit or 4-bit representations. The common LLM goal is to fit a model into less memory or increase batch capacity while preserving enough quality.
The KB verdict is practical: use quantization when a model already works but needs lower memory, lower bandwidth, or cheaper inference.

blocks.analogy: Quantization is like using a smaller measuring cup; faster to store, but you may lose fine detail.

blocks.title: Estimate weight memory from bit width
blocks.code:
params_billions = 7
for bits in [16, 8, 4]:
    gb = params_billions * 1_000_000_000 * bits / 8 / 1_000_000_000
    print(bits, "bit ->", round(gb, 1), "GB")

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the three approximate memory numbers.
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints about 14.0 GB, 7.0 GB, and 3.5 GB. Real systems add overhead, activations, and KV cache, but bit width directly changes weight storage.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

blocks.title: Check quantization
blocks.prompt: When is quantization a good first lever?

options.text: When the model lacks current facts.
When model behavior is acceptable but memory or bandwidth is the bottleneck.

blocks.explanation: Quantization optimizes deployment constraints, not missing knowledge.

modules.title: Distillation: train a smaller student
modules.sub: If repeated workload is known, transfer behavior into a cheaper model.
modules.summary: Distillation uses a teacher model or workflow to train a smaller student for a known task distribution.

blocks.title: Distillation changes the model, not just its bits

spans.text: Distillation trains a student model to imitate a stronger teacher on a known workload. The student may be smaller, faster, or easier to deploy, but it must be evaluated against both teacher and baseline.
Use distillation when you repeatedly run a capability such as routing, summarization, extraction, or grading and can collect realistic teacher outputs.

blocks.analogy: Distillation is like training an apprentice on examples from an expert until the apprentice handles routine jobs.

blocks.title: Case study: summary student for support chats

spans.text: The teacher produces high-quality summaries but costs too much for every chat. The team samples real chats, filters sensitive data, generates teacher summaries, trains a smaller student, then compares escalation-detail recall on held-out chats.

blocks.title: Check distillation
blocks.prompt: What is a major distillation risk?

options.text: The original teacher disappears from memory.
The student inherits teacher errors and may fail on production variation.

blocks.explanation: Students must be tested on held-out edge cases, not only teacher-like demos.

modules.title: Serving tactics: batch, cache, route, cap
modules.sub: Some bottlenecks live in runtime orchestration rather than model weights.
modules.summary: Batching, KV-cache management, request routing, token caps, and caching can improve cost/latency without retraining.
objectives: Connect KV cache to serving memory.
Choose routing before changing models when possible.

blocks.title: Runtime can be the bottleneck

spans.text: If quality is good and the model fits, serving tactics may be enough: continuous batching, prompt or semantic caching, shorter max output, routing simple requests to smaller models, or separating online and background work.
KV cache matters because decode stores keys and values for active sequences. Long contexts and many concurrent users can make memory scheduling the bottleneck.

blocks.analogy: Serving tactics are traffic engineering; sometimes you need better lanes, not a different car.

items.text: Short chat under 1,000 tokens: small distilled model.
Long chat with refund escalation: original model, lower concurrency.
Repeated internal test prompt: cached response.
Background weekly digest: batch job, not live endpoint.

spans.text: When an AI proposes inference optimization, inspect the bottleneck and the guardrails.

items.text: Does it measure p95 latency and quality before/after?
Does it include KV-cache or context-length memory in estimates?
Does routing preserve high-risk cases for the stronger path?
Does it define rollback when quality drops?

modules.title: Ship by quality per dollar
modules.sub: End by comparing options on the same release metric.
modules.summary: The winning optimization is the one that meets quality tolerance at lower cost or latency, with provenance and rollback.
objectives: Compare quantization, distillation, and serving tactics.

blocks.title: Optimization options head-to-head

options.name: Quantization

cells.text: Same model works but memory or bandwidth is too high.
Math, code, rare tokens, or long context may regress.
Use after full-precision quality is acceptable.

options.whenToUse: Choose for VRAM or bandwidth pressure with acceptable quality loss.

options.name: Distillation

cells.text: Known repeated workload can be imitated by a smaller model.
Student misses rare cases or inherits teacher errors.
High; needs data generation, training, evals.
Use for high-volume narrow tasks with teacher labels.

options.whenToUse: Choose when a smaller specialized model can preserve needed behavior.

options.name: Serving tactics

cells.text: Runtime scheduling, caching, or routing is the bottleneck.
Routing can send hard cases to weak paths.
Use before changing weights if orchestration can solve it.

options.whenToUse: Choose when better request handling meets the target.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the lever that solves the measured bottleneck while staying inside quality tolerance.

blocks.title: Completion problem: choose the experiment order

spans.text: The 13B summarizer is accurate but p95 latency is too high and memory limits batch size. Start with quantized loading and serving changes. Try distillation only if the workload is stable and repeated enough to justify training.

blocks.title: Check optimization

options.text: It uses the lowest bit width possible.
It meets latency or cost goals while held-out quality stays within tolerance.
It removes all expensive model calls regardless of quality.

blocks.explanation: Optimization is a product tradeoff, not a compression contest.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose quantization, distillation, serving optimization, or no ship.

llm.label: LLM
llm.laymanDefinition: A language model that predicts and generates token sequences from context.
llm.technicalNote: LLM behavior depends on training data, tokenization, context, decoding, alignment, system instructions, and the application wrapper.

token.label: Token
token.laymanDefinition: A unit of text, code, punctuation, or whitespace that the model reads and generates.
token.technicalNote: Token boundaries determine context usage, cost, latency, truncation behavior, and how the model represents text internally.

context_window.label: Context window
context_window.laymanDefinition: The limited set of input and generated tokens available to the model at one time.
context_window.technicalNote: Context windows constrain what evidence, instructions, conversation state, and tool results can influence the next output.

prompt.label: Prompt
prompt.laymanDefinition: The instructions, user request, examples, and context sent to the model.
prompt.technicalNote: Prompts are release artifacts when they shape behavior, tool use, output schema, safety handling, or evaluation results.

schema.label: Schema
schema.laymanDefinition: A machine-readable contract for fields, types, required values, and allowed shapes.
schema.technicalNote: Schemas make model outputs and tool calls checkable, but they still need validation, refusal handling, and regression tests.

tool_call.label: Tool call
tool_call.laymanDefinition: A structured request from the model to use an external capability.
tool_call.technicalNote: Tool calls should be parsed, authorized, validated, traced, and executed by trusted code rather than by free-form text.

quantization.label: Quantization
quantization.laymanDefinition: Representing model values with fewer bits to reduce memory or bandwidth.

distillation.label: Distillation
distillation.laymanDefinition: Training a smaller student model to imitate a stronger teacher.

kv_cache.label: KV cache
kv_cache.laymanDefinition: Stored keys and values reused during autoregressive decoding.

questions.why: A lesson is useful only when it changes what you do next.
